World Court Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on 19 November that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority in the northern Rakhine State. The 9-6 decision is the first time in the Court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for genocide.
The Court said the evidence pointed to around 10,000 Rohingya killed in the military's 2017 "clearance operations" and that Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants. It held that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population, which is the key legal test for genocide. In the judgement delivered on 19 November, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence against women, as well as extreme violence against children. The operations also involved the murder of infants, which Judge Iwasawa said “supports the inference that Myanmar’s security forces acted with the intent to prevent births among the group.”
The Court ordered Myanmar to cease its ongoing violations of the Genocide Convention by enacting legislation giving full effect to its obligations under the Convention and to take immediate and effective steps to investigate all persons reasonably suspected of violating the Convention and prosecute them if warranted. Myanmar must allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya to their places of residence and the reunification of families, and must compensate the Rohingya for the damages caused.
The case against Myanmar was brought by The Gambia in 2017 under the 1948 UN Genocide COnvention, which allows any state to bring a case against another state suspects of breaching the Convention. Detained activist begins dry fast for right to bail
After 21 days of her hunger strike, detained activist Wanwalee Thammasattaya has begun a dry fast to demand bail, said Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR).
Wanwalee is among the five activists sentenced on 30 October to 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge filed against them over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020. Wanwalee was denied bail along with activist-turned-reporter Phongsatorn Tancharoen, while the remaining three activists were already detained at the time of the trial.
She has been on a hunger strike since 3 November and has been admitted to the Medical Correctional Institution. She told a lawyer who visited her on 23 November that she will be going on a dry fast and will not be eating or drinking anything. She has also refused all medical treatment.
Wanwalee is seeking bail to care for sick family members. She said she is the main breadwinner of her family and keeping her detained would have an adverse impact on her family. Her lawyers have requested bail for her several times, but all requests were denied. TLHR said that the latest bail request was filed on 23 November, which the Appeal Court denied on the grounds that there is no reason to change existing order. Lawyers will appeal the denial on 25 November.

What Thailand-New Zealand relations will look like after election?
While New Zealand's strategic partnership with Thailand is expected to endure regardless of who forms the next government, a change in Wellington could bring a different emphasis to bilateral relations, particularly on human rights, climate action and regional cooperation.
New Zealand's general election has raised questions over the future direction of its foreign policy, including its growing engagement with Southeast Asia, as the country awaits the formation of a new government following a closely contested vote on 7 November.
While the partnership provides a foundation for continued cooperation, a change of government in Wellington could shift New Zealand's regional priorities, with a Labour-led administration potentially placing greater emphasis on human rights, said a policy analyst at a New Zealand-based foreign policy institute.
The election comes at an important juncture for Thailand–New Zealand relations. In August 2026, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, now serving in a caretaker capacity following the election, and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul formally elevated bilateral relations to a Strategic Partnership, setting an ambitious target of tripling two-way trade to NZ$13.5 billion by 2045.
Less than three months after formally establishing a Strategic Partnership, caretaker PM Luxon and Thai PM Anutin attended the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, on 18–19 November.
According to The Nation, Anutin was scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with Luxon during the summit. Thailand is seeking to advance cooperation in trade, investment, regional connectivity and digital technology, while APEC remains economically important to New Zealand, with member economies accounting for approximately 75% of its exports.

Veeraporn Nitiprapha: Navigating the Winding Paths of Lives and History
Walking through the giant, gray concrete pillars of Berlin’s Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, Veeraporn Nitiprapha felt her body begin to recoil.
Within minutes, the 64-year-old novelist, one of Thailand’s most celebrated literary figures and a two-time winner of the S.E.A. Write Award, was overcome by waves of dizziness, as if she were about to faint.
Her son, walking by her side, explained the memorial’s deliberate design: none of the pillars stood at a 90-degree angle. As she wandered around the area, the Stolpersteine—the brass 'stumbling stones' embedded in the pavement—grabbed her attention. The names and occupations of Holocaust victims carved onto each Stolperstein left a lasting impression on her, one that followed her all the way back to Bangkok.
“You don't see things clearly , but your body feels it immediately,” Veeraporn recalled.
Veeraporn Nitiprapha
The physical unease made her reflect on how ordinary people experienced overwhelming historical events without understanding what was happening. “They don't know what's going on. They have no clue how these things happened to them,” she said. “Most people, including future generations and even those who supported the Nazis, struggle to grasp how so many lives were extinguished.”
The encounters in Berlin led Veeraporn to repeatedly ponder how history and memories could be preserved and passed on to the next generation. “What I truly want to capture through storytelling,” she said, “is how normal people felt during uncertain times.”
Shadow of Violence Capturing these feelings through storytelling has been a long and complicated journey, shadowed by threats, confusion, and disillusionment.
At around the age of 10, Veeraporn immersed herself in Russian literature. She remembers the early 1970s as a time when bookstores were flooded with Dostoevsky, Gorky, and books of all kinds reflecting revolution and social change.

Former PM Thaksin challenges asset seizure in 17-billion baht Shin Corp tax dispute
The Central Tax Court has dismissed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra’s request for a temporary injunction to suspend the Revenue Department’s seizure of over 17 billion baht. This is the latest development in a long-running Shin Corporation tax dispute against the former PM dating back to 2006.
After a dispute of nearly 20 years including 10 years in court, the Supreme Court in 2025 ordered the former PM to pay back taxes amounting 17 billion baht related to the 2006 sales of shares in his telecom company Shin Corporation, known as Shin Corp.
On 2 July, Thaksin filed a lawsuit with the Central Tax Court against the Revenue Department, arguing that the income arising from the share sale had already been taxed. The former PM also filed a temporary injunction to suspend the asset seizure.
However, on 16 November, the request for temporary injunction was dismissed, while the preliminary hearing is expected to take place on 21 December.
The Shin Corporation tax saga The case stems from the sale of shares in Thaksin’s telecoms firm Shin Corporation on 23 January 2006, which generated a 73-billion-baht windfall for the Shinawatra family. At the time, the shares were sold to Singapore-based state-owned investment company Temasek Holdings.
In 1999, Thaksin also established another company, Ample Rich, in which he was the only shareholder. He transferred Shin Corporation shares to Ample Rich. Thaksin’s children, Pintongta and Panthongtae, later became the company’s shareholders and directors in 2005.
The controversy arose from the sale of shares that Ample Rich had held since 1999 to Pintongta and Panthongtae for only 1 baht per share.

In the early morning on Oct. 28, as students, labor groups and civic activists gathered in Jakarta and other Indonesian cities to protest a series of government policies and inaction under the hashtag #IndonesiaSadar (Indonesia aware), social media feeds swelled with three-finger salutes in diverse colors, formats and artistic interpretations. In adopting this gesture, Indonesian demonstrators drew upon imagery from pro-democracy movements across Asia.
Originally popularized by the movie The Hunger Games as a silent expression of defiance by the oppressed citizens of Panem, the three-finger salute was first adopted by student protesters in Thailand following the 2014 military coup and later that year, by demonstrators in Hong Kong during the Umbrella Movement.
The gesture resurfaced in subsequent protest waves across both jurisdictions: in Hong Kong during the 2019-2020 demonstrations as a symbol of resistance against Beijing-backed authorities and in Thailand during the 2020-2021 protests against the military-dominated government. In Thailand, it was also imbued with the French revolutionary ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, loosely translated as "No coup, liberty, democracy".
This cross-fertilization of iconography was cultivated by youth-led activist networks across Hong Kong, Taiwan and Thailand under the digital banner of the Milk Tea Alliance, a coalition united by a regional beverage culture and a shared commitment to resisting authoritarianism. The alliance subsequently expanded to Myanmar and other Southeast Asian nations, bringing its political ideals and visual vocabulary along. It was in Myanmar, in fact, that the salute achieved its most potent visual impact in the uprising against the February 2021 coup, as three-finger memes, political cartoons, and digital graphics proliferated far beyond street rallies. “Gen Z protest” takes to the street for education reform, new Constitution
On Friday afternoon (20 November), a student-led protest took place by the Democracy Monument on Ratchadamnoen Road to call for education reform, public participation for young people, and a new Constitution.
Organised by activist groups Studem Network and Free Thai Youth, the protest started at 15.00 on the foothpath in front of Satriwithaya School, later moving into the street and closing half of the roundabout around the Democracy Monument. UN Special Rapporteur calls for revise or repeal of royal defamation law following sentencing of Anon Nampa
Andrea Bolaños Vargas, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of Human Rights Defenders, has called for Thailand to impose an immediate moratorium on prosecutions and imprisonments under the royal defamation law - Section 112 of the Thai Criminal Code - and for the revise or repeal of the law to bring it in line with international human rights standards.
The call came after the Criminal Court on 30 October sentenced human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to 2 years and 8 months on a royal defamation charge over a speech delivered at a protest on 25 November 2020. On 12 November, the Appeal Court sentenced him to 4 years in prison on royal defamation and computer crimes charges for 3 Facebook posts which called for monarchy reform and criticized the use of the royal defamation law against critics of the monarchy.
Anon is now facing a cumulative prison sentence of 34 years and 5 months.
Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer in Thailand, has been in prison for more than three years. On 30 October, the Criminal Court sentenced him to another two years and eight months for speaking at a peaceful assembly. He was convicted under Thailand’s lèse-majesté law, which criminalises defaming, insulting or threatening the King, Queen, heir apparent or regent.
On 12 November, the Court of Appeal upheld another conviction against him under Section 112 of the Criminal Code and the Computer Crime Act, confirming a further four-year prison sentence. The case relates to three Facebook posts he published in January 2021 concerning the enforcement of Section 112 and monarchy reforms.
His cumulative prison sentence remains at 34 years, five months and 20 days. If he serves the full sentence, he will be in his 70s when he is released. No one should lose decades of their life for speaking out peacefully.
